Photograph: Martin Divíšek/EPA Extreme weather Extreme heat breaks temperature records in central and eastern Europe Slovakia reaches new high of 42C as authorities in Poland forced to shut down Kozienice and Połaniec power plants Europe’s dry riverbeds and scorched earth – in pictures Matthew Taylor and Ajit Niranjan Fri 7 Aug 2026 01.00 EDT Last modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 02.38 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Temperature records have been broken in several countries across central and eastern Europe as the extreme weather that has caused wildfires and droughts across the continent continues. Countries including Slovakia , Austria and Hungary registered record temperatures. On Thursday, the Slovakian hydrometeorological agency said a new high of 42C (108F) had been reached in Dolné Plachtince. Authorities in Poland were forced to shut down the Kozienice and Połaniec coal-fired power plants after critically low water levels in the Vistula River limited cooling water supplies. The disruption removed about 1.3GW of capacity from Poland’s power system. On Wednesday, the Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, had urged employers to look after their staff and provide air conditioning and cold water. View image in fullscreen Low water levels in Poland’s Vistula River on Thursday. Photograph: Wojtek Jargiło/EPA In Germany , climate activists demanding an end to the use of fossil fuels demonstrated outside the chancellery against the lack of government action to keep people safe from extreme heat. An estimated 11,900 people across the country have died from heat this summer, according to new estimates from the Robert Koch Institute. “This extreme heat and its consequences are the result of a fossil fuel policy that is completely irresponsible and extremely dangerous,” said Annkatrin Schwirten, from Fridays for Future Berlin. “We must not become accustomed to thousands of heat-related deaths every summer.” The Hungarian prime minister, Péter Magyar, wrote on X on Thursday that the nuclear power station which had been temporarily powered down would be going back online. “Good news: we are already nine centimeters above the Danube’s Sunday low point, and rain is expected in the Austrian catchment areas,” he wrote. “One of the turbines at the Paks nuclear power plant is operating. Regardless of this, on today’s hot day there will still be a strong need for voluntary reductions in electricity consumption.” The brutal heat and continuing drought conditions are being supercharged by the escalating climate crisis , and experts warn these are putting huge pressure on local populations, critical infrastructure and wildlife across the region. Paweł Pomian, from EKO-UNIA, a Polish environmental organisation, said “power plants driving climate change were increasingly becoming its victims”, adding that the impact of this summer’s extreme conditions, fuelled by the burning of fossil fuels, should be a “wake-up call not only for Poland, but for the whole of Europe”. “The faster we develop wind and solar power – technologies that require the least water to generate electricity – the better we can protect both energy security and our rivers,” he said. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment Preview latest after newsletter promotion View image in fullscreen Environmental experts examine part of the Danube riverbed in Budapest on Thursday. Photograph: Attila Kisbenedek/AFP/Getty Images The scorching heatwaves have also deprived vegetation of moisture and primed much of the continent for wildfires. About half a million hectares have burned across the EU since the start of the year, mostly in Spain and France, according to data published by the European Forest Fire Information System on Thursday. A further 292,000 hectares (721,000 acres) have burned in Ukraine. We launched a war on nature. Now we are in a climate warzone | Rebecca Solnit Read more The severity of fire weather – the hot, dry and windy conditions that make it harder to battle blazes when they break out – has set new records for the time of year, by alarming margins in some countries. In Austria, which had a record high temperature of 41.2C on Wednesday, cumulative fire weather is more than twice as severe as the previous record for this time of year. In Czechia , which registered a new national temperature record earlier in the summer, fire weather by early August was more than 50% worse than the previous record, and in Slovakia it was 32% worse. Last week, a rapid analysis by the World Weather Attribution consortium found that global heating had made last month’s hot, dry and windy weather at least 20 times more likely in Spain and twice as likely in France. https://londonlovesbusiness.com/polish-s.text: Tech Property Business London Loves Leszek Szymański / - / Avalon Business News Defence Politics News World News Polish security chief fights for life after mysterious embassy fall as Russia tensions rise by Defence Correspondent September 21, 2026 written by Defence Correspondent 21 st Sep 26 9:59 am A senior Polish diplomatic security official is fighting for his life after falling from a third-floor window at a Polish diplomatic compound in Ljubljana, an unexplained incident that has raised questions in Warsaw as tensions between Russia and NATO escalate. The official, who works for Poland’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, fell during the early hours of September 13 and remains in critical condition in a Slovenian hospital, according to reports citing Polish authorities. Poland’s foreign ministry confirmed the incident, but details remain limited. Slovenian police were notified of the incident but did not inspect the premises. Diplomatic premises are protected by international law and local authorities cannot enter without permission from the diplomatic mission. Slovenian police said: “According to the information collected so far, for a currently unknown reason, a person fell from a balcony and was seriously injured. His life is in danger. “We were informed by the diplomatic mission that their competent investigators will carry out the procedural actions themselves, including inspecting the scene and investigating the circumstances of the incident.” The official was reportedly on holiday at the time. Polish media have also reported that he had taken possession of a diplomatic pouch despite not having official authorisation to undertake the related duty. Those details have not established any connection between the incident and his professional role. Reports have also suggested that several people were present at a gathering when the diplomat fell. Slovenian reporting has stressed that significant details remain unclear, including precisely what happened immediately before the fall. Krzysztof Bosak, deputy speaker of Poland’s parliament, has described the circumstances as “suspicious” and called for a detailed investigation. He said: “If [a security employee] falls out of a window in a building and it turns out that they were on vacation and were carrying some kind of parcel, then it is no longer a case of mystery.” There is currently no evidence establishing that the fall was connected to espionage, sabotage or the official’s security responsibilities. Nor has there been any public allegation that Russia was involved. The incident has nevertheless emerged at a particularly sensitive moment for Poland, one of Nato’s most exposed eastern members and a major logistical hub for Western military assistance to Ukraine. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has warned that Moscow could seek to test NATO’s willingness to respond to attacks or other hostile operations against countries supporting Ukraine. The warning comes as European intelligence officials have raised concerns about possible Russian provocations against NATO in the coming months, including drone or missile attacks, sabotage and operations targeting critical infrastructure. Poland has also repeatedly scrambled aircraft in response to Russian attacks close to its borders. On September 17, Polish fighter jets were deployed after a major Russian missile and drone assault on Ukraine, although Warsaw said there had been no breach of Polish airspace on that occasion. A Polish military spokesman said on Friday: “Ground-based air defence systems and radar reconnaissance systems are at a state of readiness. The heightened alert reflects a broader change in the security environment across Nato’s eastern flank. European governments are increasingly preparing for scenarios in which conventional military operations could be accompanied by cyber attacks , drone incursions, sabotage and disruption to energy and communications infrastructure. Tusk has also warned about what he sees as growing political divisions inside Europe over support for Ukraine, arguing that parties such as France’s National Rally and Germany’s AfD advocate peace while also supporting positions that would amount to Ukrainian capitulation. The debate is unfolding as European governments face pressure to increase defence spending and strengthen their ability to respond without relying entirely on American military capabilities. Ezra Cohen, who served as Acting Under-Secretary of Defence for Intelligence and Security during Donald Trump’s first term as US president, said: “If European countries step up, the US is going to be there with them. We need countries like Germany and France to get serious.” For Poland, the immediate issue remains the unexplained fall of a senior security official and his condition. The absence of a Slovenian police investigation has added to the unanswered questions, but diplomatic immunity does not itself imply wrongdoing or foreign involvement. The Polish investigation will have to establish whether the incident was an accident or whether other circumstances were involved. For now, the case remains unresolved — even as the wider European security environment becomes increasingly tense. The distinction matters: heightened concern over Russian activity across Europe provides the geopolitical backdrop, but it does not establish a link between that activity and the incident in Ljubljana. https://www.naturalnews.com/2026-09-27-o.text: According to the column, Moscow has repeatedly declared it has no intention of attacking NATO or the U.K., and those declarations are ignored. The article states that the campaign frames any conflict as strictly defensive and tells the population it must prepare to withstand and resist a Russian attack. The column cites parallel developments in France, where President Emmanuel Macron called a meeting on "Russian hybrid warfare," and in Germany, where officials and media have focused on a drone incident at Leipzig-Halle airport. The piece was published under RT 's opinion section and carries a disclaimer that the views expressed are solely those of the author. U.K. Figures and Media Cited The column names former Conservative minister Jacob Rees-Mogg as making what it calls the most grotesque contribution, citing his remarks about "circumstances where people may have to die" and an analogy to the fall of Rome. Amar writes that Rees-Mogg's reference to paying others to fight and die may be a "Freudian slip" given Western support for Ukraine. The article points to Sky News ' four-part docudrama "The Wargame," which it says is built on the premise that Russia is about to attack and features former politicians Michael Gove and Nicola Sturgeon. It quotes British Chief of the Defense Staff Air Chief Marshal Sir Richard Knighton referring to a "national conversation on defense" and saying the purpose is to remedy "what the British public hasn't got, [...] haven't understood." Amar describes Knighton's approach as patronizing and "positively Orwellian," and notes Knighton held up Estonia and Sweden as examples of societies where threat awareness is part of daily life. The column also references a report that the British government is dusting off a classified Cold War manual, telling households to stockpile canned food and bottled water at home, while state media puts out articles debating whether the country is mentally prepared for war, according to Modernity News [1]. European Context and Counterpoints The article states that Estonian authorities, despite generally hawkish views on Russia, have called on NATO and European Union countries to reduce alarmism. It quotes Estonian officials saying the Russia-at-the-gates narrative "has been blown completely out of proportion" and that "there is absolutely no reason to believe that Russia is imminently going to launch a military attack on NATO, Estonia or the Baltic states." Amar argues that war propaganda is almost immune to its own absurdities and inconsistencies because it operates on fear, stereotypes, and conformism rather than reason. This observation aligns with research on human threat management systems, which shows that fear-related responses can override rational assessment of danger [2]. The column also asserts that some British establishment members want to reinforce conformism by locking up dissenters, though it does not provide specific names or legal proposals. The broader European context includes what Amar describes as similar establishment-induced hysteria across much of NATO-EU Europe. In Germany, the drone affair at Leipzig-Halle airport has been repeatedly stirred by Berlin and its mainstream media, though Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova dismissed the allegation as baseless, stating that "this whole drone story is based on nothing: there are no facts, no supporting materials, absolutely zero, nothing" [3]. Author's Conclusions and Dissent Amar writes that U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham used his first UN General Assembly address to blame Britain's problems on Russia rather than on his predecessor Keir Starmer. The article states that social media shows signs many Britons do not appreciate efforts to scare and mobilize them for what the author calls a senseless war. Amar concludes that the "elites" are insane and malevolent, and that any hope for peace and a return to reason will have to come from below. The column reflects a broader pattern of establishment messaging that critics say relies on psychological manipulation rather than factual threat assessment, a concern echoed in analyses of media influence on public perception [4]. Conclusion The RT column presents an opinion-based account alleging a coordinated U.K. establishment campaign to prepare the public for war with Russia, citing Rees-Mogg, Knighton, Sky NewsÂ and European examples. It also cites Estonian officials who dispute the imminence of any Russian attack, and it includes RT 's standard disclaimer that the views are the author's alone. No independent verification of the column's claims was provided in the article, and the assertions remain attributed to Amar and the sources he quotes. The piece reflects ongoing tensions in public discourse over threat perception and the role of media in shaping public attitudes toward military conflict. References Modernity News. https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/16/puti.text: Russian President Vladimir Putin has signed a decree ordering the compulsory seizure of Russian assets belonging to French flooring manufacturer Tarkett and four other European companies, whose combined annual revenue exceeds 50 billion roubles (€532 million).The assets have been placed under the interim control of a management company called Centre Capital, registered in February 2026.Its chief executive is listed as Marat Mirkhaydarov, former head of the administration of the regional governor of Zabaykalsky, who stood down in 2025 following an injury sustained in Russia's ongoing war in Ukraine.The decree also covers paper packaging producer Kappa Rus, formerly part of Ireland's Smurfit Kappa, hygiene product maker Ontex RU, part of the Belgian Ontex group, metal packaging manufacturer Eviosys Packaging Kuban, part of US-based Sonoco Products Company, and Menshen Packaging CIS, owned by German plastics producer Menshen.All five companies continued operating in Russia after the country's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.Tarkett, which ranks third globally by floor covering sales and leads the market in vinyl flooring according to its 2024 annual report, kept two plants in Russia out of its 34 production sites worldwide and continued paying taxes to the Russian budget.The latest seizures follow a series of similar moves in September, when Putin placed the Russian assets of Swiss food giant Nestlé, German hypermarket chain Metro, French retailer Auchan and home improvement chain Leroy Merlin under temporary administration.Those assets were transferred to a company called LEV Management, established shortly before the decision and reported by Russian media to have links to the country's security services. A manufacturer of plastic dispensing systems owned by French holding Aptar Europe Holding was also placed under temporary administration shortly afterwards.A presidential decree signed in April 2023 established the mechanism for such seizures, authorising the imposition of temporary administration over certain Russian assets of foreign companies.Western governments and international legal experts have described the move as unlawful expropriation. Companies whose assets are seized can, in principle, pursue compensation through international arbitration under bilateral investment treaties Russia has signed with EU member states, although enforcing judgments against the Kremlin and its entities is nearly impossible.The first targets under that decree were Danish brewer Carlsberg and French dairy group Danone.Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov directly linked the transfer of Nestlé's and Auchan's assets to the fact that they are companies from what Moscow terms "unfriendly countries".“Unfriendly countries” is an official Russian government designation applied to all EU member states, the US, the UK and other states that imposed sanctions following the 2022 full-scale invasion, in an attempt to dissuade them from aiding Kyiv.Russia has framed the asset seizures in part as a response to the EU’s decision to freeze approximately €300 billion in Russian sovereign assets following the all-out invasion.

https://dailypioneer.com/news/russian-dr.text: At least two people were killed and several crew members, including an Indian national, were injured after a Russian drone strike triggered a fire aboard a Turkish-owned civilian cargo vessel in the Black Sea, authorities said..The Indian Embassy in Romania said three Indian nationals were among the crew and that one of them was injured and receiving medical treatment.."We have learnt of an attack today on commercial vessel MV ROYAD MAMMADOV in the Black Sea. As per preliminary information, there have been 2 casualties (foreign nationals) while some crew members have been injured and are undergoing medical treatment in Romania. It is further reported that there are three Indian nationals among the crew members," the mission said in a post on X..The embassy said it was coordinating with relevant authorities to gather more information about the safety and wellbeing of the Indian crew members..Indian Ambassador Manoj Mohapatra subsequently spoke to the three Indian nationals and confirmed that they were all in good health.."Amb @manojifs spoke with the three Indian nationals receiving treatment at Constanța County Hospital. He also spoke with the hospital’s Chief Physician, who confirmed that all three are in good health and receiving necessary care. The Ambassador assured them of all possible assistance and support," the mission said..The embassy later reiterated that all three Indian nationals were safe.."We have spoken to them. One of them has been injured and is receiving medical attention. We are in close touch with the hospital authorities. We are extending all possible support for the welfare and wellbeing of the Indian crew members," it said..The nationalities of the two people who died were not immediately available..Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, meanwhile, said on Monday that two Russian drones had carried out a "horrific strike" on a civilian vessel in neutral waters that was carrying corn and owned by Turkiye.."Azerbaijani and Indian citizens were on board.
